morningSummary:
Tuesday, 17 November 2026 — Morning News & Global Update. Checked at 08:02, Europe/Paris. The day's leading international developments span the security of the Strait of Hormuz, a planned meeting of the leaders of the United States, China and Russia, political accountability in Nigeria and Washington, France's public-sector pay dispute, and a new debate over the future of the UK's relationship with the European Union.

MIDDLE EAST, ENERGY AND GLOBAL MARKETS — The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency has recorded an unidentified projectile striking a merchant vessel near the Strait of Hormuz. The warning does not identify the attacker or establish the weapon used. Oman and Iran have separately discussed protecting maritime corridors, but no agreement restoring normal commercial passage has been announced. Oil prices eased in early trading: Reuters reported Brent at US$91.66 and US WTI at US$84.99. Expectations of a fourth-quarter supply surplus have outweighed immediate security concerns, although Hormuz shipping remains disrupted and the region remains vulnerable to further incidents. Japan's proposal for an Asia-wide oil-security task force is a response to the same vulnerability.

ASIA AND GREAT-POWER DIPLOMACY — Donald Trump is beginning an Asia trip in Manila, where a Quad leaders' meeting involving the United States, Japan, Australia and India is expected to address maritime security, critical minerals, export controls and artificial intelligence. China has confirmed a planned Xi Jinping–Donald Trump–Vladimir Putin summit in Shenzhen on 19 November. No agreed agenda or outcome has been announced. Japan's Ministry of Defense says two suspected Russian aircraft briefly entered Japanese territorial airspace near Okinoshima; Tokyo scrambled fighters and lodged a strong protest. The aircraft were described as suspected Russian aircraft, and the ministry did not publish their types. Canada and China have expanded a preliminary trade arrangement: Beijing will reduce tariffs on about C$400 million of Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports, while Canada extends tariff-remission measures for some Chinese steel and aluminium products for two years.

NIGERIA — Annual headline inflation eased to 14.06% in October from 14.63% in September, while food inflation fell to 19.13%. This is a slower rate of price increases, not a fall in the overall price level. The proposed state-police constitutional amendment has advanced after Senate Leader Opeyemi Bamidele said 32 state assemblies had approved it; four reports were still expected. The final legal text, funding, oversight and safeguards against political misuse remain central questions. In opposition politics, Nafiu Bala Gombe has offered conditional reconciliation to Atiku Abubakar and David Mark, but no settlement has been announced. The Mark-led faction's appeal and stay application do not automatically suspend the 5 November judgment; no appellate stay or final appeal outcome was verified for this edition. INEC has said it will review the certified judgment and take legal advice. The Presidency has also directed the release of 78 suspects arrested after an attack on President Tinubu's convoy, according to the FCT police; the police say the suspects are to be warned and released. Separately, NDC figures have called for transparent information about federal health-budget releases. Peter Obi's campaign has reported disruption and attacks around NDC activities; the APC has condemned violence and denied involvement in specific allegations. No independent finding reviewed for this edition establishes who organised the incidents. The Kwankwaso convoy account also remains disputed. Nigeria says US intelligence-sharing, satellite imagery and training are supporting military operations against armed groups; official claims about battlefield results should be assessed against independent evidence.

AFRICA — Provisional results from the DRC Ebola response remain serious: the ECDC's 16 November update recorded 11,376 confirmed cases and 5,568 related deaths using data through 14 November. Nigeria's single reported case was discharged on 11 November and all 62 identified contacts completed monitoring. In Sudan, a local rights group says an army airstrike killed at least 13 people in West Kordofan; the Associated Press could not independently verify the toll, and an army-aligned spokesperson said forces had targeted RSF positions without directly addressing the civilian-death report. Sudan and Ethiopia are also accusing each other of backing armed opponents. Both governments deny the allegations, which AP says it could not independently verify. In The Gambia, the electoral commission has cleared President Adama Barrow and eight other candidates to contest the December presidential election; the clearance is not an election result.

FRANCE AND EUROPE — Public-sector unions representing France's civil service have called a national strike and demonstrations on 17 November over pay and purchasing power. Eight unions are involved; the government has opened a one-month discussion on targeted measures but has not agreed to a general increase in the civil-service index point, frozen since July 2023. Marine Le Pen is due to present pension proposals today. The National Rally says its plan could save €15–20 billion annually while allowing some early starters to retire at 60–62, but investors question how those savings can be reconciled with reversing the 2023 pension reform. These are opposition campaign proposals, not government policy or independently verified savings. France's growth is expected to remain weak, with household purchasing power under pressure. Across the EU, foreign ministers have imposed new sanctions on nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions and say a ceasefire should precede a durable peace agreement. Moscow disputes claims that it has agreed to European participation in the next round of Ukraine talks. In Turkey, Reuters reports that police raided pro-opposition Sözcü TV and that a trustee was appointed; prosecutors' reported financial and political allegations remain under investigation, not proof of guilt. In the UK, Prime Minister Andy Burnham's 16 November speech said Brexit had weakened Britain's global standing. He wants practical agreements at the 20 November summit and a longer discussion about the UK's future relationship with the EU; no immediate return to the bloc has been announced.

UNITED STATES, CANADA AND TECHNOLOGY — Democrats won both chambers of Congress in the 2026 midterms, but the new majority does not take office until January 2027. The White House has warned that planned investigations could amount to criminality; Democrats say congressional oversight is a constitutional duty. The dispute is a political and legal argument, not a finding of wrongdoing. New US licensing rules are intended to stop restricted AI computing power reaching Chinese firms through overseas data centres and third-country chip sales. The rules may affect investment and compliance costs in Southeast Asia. The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development's Transition Report 2026–27 warns that developing economies risk missing AI and defence-sector opportunities without reliable power, finance, skills and industrial capacity. UN talks in Geneva also remain divided over whether to negotiate binding limits on lethal autonomous weapons.

BUSINESS, CLIMATE AND PUBLIC INTEREST — Japan's economy contracted at an annualised 0.1% in the July–September quarter, reflecting weak household demand and external pressures. Renault plans 1,090 voluntary departures in France while hiring in digital and engineering roles, according to Le Monde. COP31 negotiations continue over climate action and the wording of a draft decision on fossil fuels. RadiantWaves will distinguish official data, attributed allegations, provisional results, campaign promises and proposals still under negotiation. Repository photographs are used where available; contextual images are labelled as illustrations rather than event photographs. featured.title: Gombe offers conditional reconciliation to Atiku and David Mark as ADC leadership dispute continues
featured.summary: Nafiu Bala Gombe says he is willing to work with Atiku Abubakar and David Mark, but insists that party membership rules and constitutional procedures be respected. No settlement or appellate stay has been announced.
featured.content: Nafiu Bala Gombe, whose lawsuit produced the 5 November Federal High Court judgment affecting the David Mark-led ADC leadership, has offered conditional reconciliation to Atiku Abubakar, David Mark and other party figures. In an interview with BBC Hausa, reported by Premium Times, Gombe said he did not want the judgment used to victimise members of the rival faction. He nevertheless insists that anyone seeking leadership or nomination must comply with the party constitution, including ward registration and membership-dues requirements. The Mark-led faction has appealed and applied for a stay of execution, arguing that the court lacked jurisdiction. An appeal or stay application does not automatically suspend a judgment; no appellate stay or final appeal outcome was verified for this edition. INEC has said it will review the certified judgment and take legal advice. The dispute affects party leadership, earlier decisions and the route to the ADC's 2027 presidential nomination.

topStories.title: UK maritime monitor reports an unidentified projectile strike near Hormuz as Oman and Iran discuss shipping safety
topStories.summary: UKMTO recorded an unidentified projectile striking a merchant vessel near the Strait of Hormuz. Oman and Iran have discussed maritime safety, but no deal restoring normal passage has been announced and the attacker has not been identified.
topStories.content: The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency recorded an unidentified projectile striking a merchant vessel near the Strait of Hormuz in Warning 207-26. The warning does not identify the attacker, establish the weapon used or provide grounds for attributing responsibility. Separately, Oman's Foreign Ministry said Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi and Omani officials discussed safeguarding maritime corridors, maintaining the flow of global shipping and reviving dialogue to prevent escalation. Oman has long acted as a mediator and is strategically positioned beside the strait. The talks are important, but they are not a confirmed agreement to reopen normal commercial passage. Ship operators continue to face security warnings, uncertain routes and the possibility of higher freight and insurance costs. Any assessment of the incident must distinguish the UKMTO report of an impact from unverified claims about who was responsible.

topStories.title: Trump begins Asia tour with Quad meeting in Manila before China visit
topStories.country: United States / Philippines / India / Japan / Australia / China
topStories.summary: Donald Trump is due in Manila for the first Quad leaders' meeting in two years, ahead of an APEC gathering in Shenzhen. Maritime security, critical minerals, export controls and artificial intelligence are among the expected topics.
topStories.content: US President Donald Trump is travelling to the Philippines as part of an Asia tour that includes a meeting of the Quad — the United States, Japan, Australia and India — and the APEC forum in Shenzhen, China. Reuters reports that the Quad leaders' meeting is the group's first in two years. The agenda is expected to include maritime security, export controls, critical-mineral supply chains and artificial intelligence. The visit comes after Republican losses in US midterm elections and amid renewed scrutiny of a fragile US-China trade truce. Demonstrations in Manila have also criticised the Middle East war and the US-led Pax Silica initiative. Trump is expected to meet Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr and take part in a US-ASEAN special summit, while the Shenzhen programme is expected to bring him into contact with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The trip is a test of whether Washington can reassure regional partners while keeping economic and security channels open with Beijing. Planned meetings should not be treated as completed agreements until official readouts are issued.

topStories.title: France's public-sector unions stage nationwide strike over pay and purchasing power
topStories.summary: Eight public-sector unions have called a national strike and demonstrations on 17 November over pay and purchasing power. The government has offered targeted measures for lower-paid staff but has not agreed to a general increase in the civil-service index point.
topStories.content: Eight public-sector unions in France — CGT, FO, CFDT, UNSA, FSU, Solidaires, CFE-CGC and FA-FP — have called workers to strike and demonstrate on Tuesday, 17 November. Their central demand is an immediate improvement in pay and a rise in the civil-service index point, which has been frozen since July 2023. Le Monde reports that the unions regard the government's targeted measures for lower-paid employees as insufficient, particularly because the minimum-wage increase due on 1 December will leave the base pay of many public employees below the new SMIC. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has opened a one-month discussion on five areas, including emergency measures for low salaries, and has scheduled another meeting with unions for 11 December. The government argues that a general increase would be costly and is prioritising targeted support. The scale of participation and disruption to schools, transport and public services is still being assessed; local effects will vary. The mobilisation is a labour dispute and should not be presented as a general call for the government's resignation.

topStories.title: Canada and China extend trade concessions as Carney seeks alternatives to US market dependence
topStories.summary: Canada and China have expanded a preliminary trade arrangement. Beijing will reduce tariffs on about C$400 million of Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports, while Ottawa extends tariff-remission measures for some Chinese steel and aluminium products for two years.
topStories.content: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to extend and expand a preliminary trade arrangement during a meeting in Shenzhen ahead of the APEC summit. Reuters reports that China will reduce tariffs on about C$400 million of Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports. Canada will extend for two years remission measures for some Chinese steel and aluminium products. Carney said Canada was ahead of schedule on its goal of increasing exports to China by 50% by 2030, as his government seeks to diversify markets and reduce dependence on the United States. The arrangement is not a comprehensive free-trade agreement. It also does not erase concerns raised by security analysts and human-rights groups about alleged Chinese election interference, coercive trade practices and the treatment of dissidents. Beijing rejects accusations of interference in Canada's domestic affairs. The trade concessions create opportunities for exporters, but implementation and domestic political scrutiny will matter.

topStories.whyItMatters: The arrangement could help Canadian farmers and seafood exporters, but it also raises questions about supply-chain dependence, strategic industries and the balance between trade diversification and security.

topStories.title: EU accuses Russia of prolonging Ukraine war and imposes new sanctions
topStories.summary: EU foreign ministers accused Moscow of dragging out peace talks while attacking Ukrainian infrastructure and agreed sanctions targeting nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions, alongside individuals and energy-linked business interests.
topStories.content: European Union foreign ministers meeting in Brussels accused Russia of prolonging negotiations over Ukraine while continuing attacks on power plants and other infrastructure as winter approaches. The Associated Press reports that the EU imposed sanctions on nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions and targeted energy- and oil-linked businesspeople, as well as people accused of spreading pro-Russian disinformation. Ministers said a ceasefire should come before a lasting peace agreement and rejected a Russian-proposed European security framework that they regard as an attempt to weaken NATO. US-led contacts have not produced a lasting ceasefire, and major disagreements remain over territory and future security guarantees. EU leaders have agreed that advisers from France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy and Poland, together with EU officials, should represent Europe in future discussions. The proposed format is not a peace deal. Ukraine's sovereignty and its own decisions remain central to any settlement.

topStories.title: Sudan rights group reports at least 13 killed in West Kordofan airstrike
topStories.summary: Emergency Lawyers says a Sudanese army airstrike killed at least 13 people, including women and children, in West Kordofan. The Associated Press says it could not independently verify the reported death toll.
topStories.content: A local rights group, Emergency Lawyers, says at least 13 people were killed when a Sudanese army airstrike hit the Abu Qalb area of West Kordofan. Women and children were among those reported dead, and several homes were said to have been destroyed. The Associated Press could not independently verify the death toll. A spokesperson for forces aligned with the army said troops had entered the area and eliminated Rapid Support Forces positions, but did not directly address the reported civilian deaths. Sudan's war between the army and the RSF began in April 2023 and has caused mass displacement, widespread destruction and severe food insecurity. Aid organisations estimate that at least 59,000 people have been killed and around 13 million displaced. The report underscores the risks to civilians as fighting and drone warfare spread across Kordofan and other regions. Responsibility for the specific reported civilian deaths remains disputed and requires independent investigation.

topStories.title: Sudan-Ethiopia tensions rise as both governments trade accusations over armed groups
topStories.summary: Sudan and Ethiopia accuse each other of supporting armed opponents. Both governments deny the allegations, which the Associated Press says it could not independently verify; diplomatic expulsions and border tensions have increased.
topStories.content: Relations between Sudan and Ethiopia have deteriorated as the two governments exchange accusations about support for armed groups operating in each other's territory. Sudan alleges that Ethiopia is hosting camps and enabling the Rapid Support Forces to launch drone and cross-border operations. Ethiopia accuses Sudan of supporting Tigrayan rebels after clashes resumed in September. Both sides deny the allegations, and the Associated Press says it could not independently verify them. Sudan has raised its claims with the United Nations and African Union, while Ethiopia has expelled six Sudanese consular staff and closed the mission. The dispute is unfolding alongside Sudan's devastating war and renewed fighting in Tigray. Analysts warn that cross-border weapons movements and proxy activity could widen the instability. The allegations must remain attributed claims rather than established facts. Regional diplomacy is urgently needed to prevent the two conflicts from becoming more closely connected.

topStories.title: White House warns Democrats over planned probes as new Congress prepares to take control
topStories.summary: After Democrats won both chambers in the 2026 midterms, White House counsel warned that planned investigations could amount to criminality. Democrats say congressional oversight is a constitutional duty; the new Congress takes office in January 2027.
topStories.content: The White House has warned Democrats that planned investigations into the Trump administration could amount to what it called “blatant criminality”, escalating a dispute over congressional oversight before the new Congress takes office in January 2027. The Associated Press reports that White House counsel Will Scharf sent a letter to Representative Robert Garcia, the expected incoming House Oversight Committee chair, after Garcia said Trump officials should prepare for scrutiny. Democrats plan investigations into the administration's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files, immigration enforcement, White House construction projects, mineral deals and cryptocurrency activity, among other matters. Garcia rejected the administration's warning and said Congress has constitutional authority to investigate potential wrongdoing. Current Republican committee chair James Comer has also stressed the committee's independence. Democrats won control of both the House and Senate in the midterms, but Republicans remain in control during the lame-duck period until the new Congress is sworn in on 3 January 2027. The White House's warning is a political and legal argument, not a finding that any planned investigation is criminal.

topStories.title: New US AI-chip export controls unsettle Southeast Asian data-centre investment
topStories.country: United States / Singapore / Malaysia / Thailand / Indonesia / Brazil
topStories.summary: New US licensing rules require overseas data centres serving firms in China, Russia, Iran and Cuba to identify end users, and add licensing requirements for chip shipments to several countries including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.
topStories.content: The Trump administration has introduced new export-control requirements intended to prevent Chinese companies from obtaining restricted American AI computing power through overseas cloud providers. The Associated Press reports that data centres outside the United States serving companies in China, Russia, Iran and Cuba must identify end users, while chip sales to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil face additional licensing requirements because US officials regard those routes as higher risk for diversion. The measures follow scrutiny of possible diversion of Nvidia chips through third-country data centres. Singapore and Malaysia are reviewing possible rerouting of servers and chips and are engaging with US authorities. The controls may raise compliance costs and affect regional data-centre investment, but they are not a general ban on all AI services in Southeast Asia. Firms will need to distinguish lawful cloud access from transactions that require licences or enhanced customer checks.

topStories.title: Ebola outbreak in DR Congo exceeds 11,000 reported cases as Nigeria completes contact monitoring
topStories.country: Democratic Republic of Congo; Uganda; South Sudan; Nigeria
topStories.summary: The ECDC's 16 November update recorded 11,376 confirmed cases and 5,568 related deaths in the DRC, using data through 14 November. Nigeria's single reported case was discharged on 11 November and all 62 identified contacts completed monitoring.
topStories.content: The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control's 16 November update recorded 11,376 confirmed cases and 5,568 related deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, using data available through 14 November. Community transmission continues across eight provinces. The update also says one Ebola case was reported in Nigeria on 20 October in a person with travel history to Uganda; the patient was medically evacuated to Switzerland and discharged on 11 November. All 62 identified contacts in Nigeria completed monitoring on 11 November, while one contact remained in quarantine in Switzerland. Kenya had reported nine confirmed cases, including two deaths, all linked to its first case; the last case was reported on 20 October. These figures are tied to the ECDC's reporting cut-off and should not be presented as real-time totals. Nigeria's completed contact monitoring is reassuring, but it does not remove the need for surveillance, infection prevention and cross-border coordination.

topStories.title: Japan proposes an Asia-wide oil-security task force after Hormuz disruption exposes supply risks
topStories.summary: Japan has proposed an Asia-wide task force to coordinate oil stockpiles and emergency releases, potentially using spare storage capacity in Japan and working with a Philippine-led scheme.
topStories.content: Japan has proposed an Asia-wide oil-security task force to coordinate strategic stockpiles and emergency supply releases after the conflict around the Strait of Hormuz exposed the region's dependence on Gulf energy. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told Southeast Asian leaders in Manila that Japan could make use of idle storage capacity and work with a Philippine-led joint stockpiling scheme. She described the idea as a possible Asian counterpart to the International Energy Agency and also proposed a Power Gulf Initiative to strengthen ties between Middle Eastern producers and Asian consumers. Reuters reports that around 90% of crude oil shipped through the Strait of Hormuz is destined for Asia. The proposal is not yet an operating regional reserve or a binding commitment to release oil. It would require agreed membership, financing, access rules, information-sharing and emergency procedures.

worldNews.summary: UKMTO recorded an unidentified projectile striking a merchant vessel near the Strait of Hormuz. Oman and Iran have discussed maritime safety, but no deal restoring normal passage has been announced and the attacker has not been identified.
worldNews.content: The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency recorded an unidentified projectile striking a merchant vessel near the Strait of Hormuz in Warning 207-26. Separately, Oman's Foreign Ministry said Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi and Omani officials discussed safeguarding maritime corridors, maintaining the flow of global shipping and reviving dialogue to prevent escalation. Oman has long acted as a mediator and is strategically positioned beside the strait. The talks are important, but they are not a confirmed agreement to reopen normal commercial passage. Ship operators continue to face security warnings, uncertain routes and the possibility of higher freight and insurance costs. Any assessment of the incident must distinguish the UKMTO report of an impact from unverified claims about who was responsible.

worldNews.title: EU accuses Russia of prolonging Ukraine war and imposes new sanctions
worldNews.summary: EU foreign ministers accused Moscow of dragging out peace talks while attacking Ukrainian infrastructure and agreed sanctions targeting nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions, alongside individuals and energy-linked business interests.
worldNews.content: European Union foreign ministers meeting in Brussels accused Russia of prolonging negotiations over Ukraine while continuing attacks on power plants and other infrastructure as winter approaches. The Associated Press reports that the EU imposed sanctions on nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions and targeted energy- and oil-linked businesspeople, as well as people accused of spreading pro-Russian disinformation. Ministers said a ceasefire should come before a lasting peace agreement and rejected a Russian-proposed European security framework that they regard as an attempt to weaken NATO. US-led contacts have not produced a lasting ceasefire, and major disagreements remain over territory and future security guarantees. EU leaders have agreed that advisers from France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy and Poland, together with EU officials, should represent Europe in future discussions. The proposed format is not a peace deal. Ukraine's sovereignty and its own decisions remain central to any settlement.

worldNews.title: Sudan rights group reports at least 13 killed in West Kordofan airstrike
worldNews.summary: Emergency Lawyers says a Sudanese army airstrike killed at least 13 people, including women and children, in West Kordofan. The Associated Press says it could not independently verify the reported death toll.
worldNews.content: A local rights group, Emergency Lawyers, says at least 13 people were killed when a Sudanese army airstrike hit the Abu Qalb area of West Kordofan. Women and children were among those reported dead, and several homes were said to have been destroyed. The Associated Press could not independently verify the death toll. A spokesperson for forces aligned with the army said troops had entered the area and eliminated Rapid Support Forces positions, but did not directly address the reported civilian deaths. Sudan's war between the army and the RSF began in April 2023 and has caused mass displacement, widespread destruction and severe food insecurity. Aid organisations estimate that at least 59,000 people have been killed and around 13 million displaced. The report underscores the risks to civilians as fighting and drone warfare spread across Kordofan and other regions. Responsibility for the specific reported civilian deaths remains disputed and requires independent investigation.

worldNews.title: Sudan-Ethiopia tensions rise as both governments trade accusations over armed groups
worldNews.summary: Sudan and Ethiopia accuse each other of supporting armed opponents. Both governments deny the allegations, which the Associated Press says it could not independently verify; diplomatic expulsions and border tensions have increased.
worldNews.content: Relations between Sudan and Ethiopia have deteriorated as the two governments exchange accusations about support for armed groups operating in each other's territory. Sudan alleges that Ethiopia is hosting camps and enabling the Rapid Support Forces to launch drone and cross-border operations. Ethiopia accuses Sudan of supporting Tigrayan rebels after clashes resumed in September. Both sides deny the allegations, and the Associated Press says it could not independently verify them. Sudan has raised its claims with the United Nations and African Union, while Ethiopia has expelled six Sudanese consular staff and closed the mission. The dispute is unfolding alongside Sudan's devastating war and renewed fighting in Tigray. Analysts warn that cross-border weapons movements and proxy activity could widen the instability. The allegations must remain attributed claims rather than established facts. Regional diplomacy is urgently needed to prevent the two conflicts from becoming more closely connected.

Israeli authorities say security screening is necessary to prevent weapons and materials reaching armed groups; humanitarian agencies argue that delays and restrictions are preventing aid from reaching civilians at the scale required. The latest diplomatic call does not itself change border procedures or guarantee additional deliveries. Aid organisations continue to stress that civilians must be protected and that humanitarian access should be safe, sustained and independent of political bargaining.

worldNews.title: UN Geneva talks remain divided over legally binding limits on autonomous weapons
worldNews.country: Switzerland / United States / Russia / Israel / European states
worldNews.summary: States meeting in Geneva remain divided over whether to negotiate a binding protocol on lethal autonomous weapons. The US, Russia and Israel oppose a binding pact; several European states support negotiations.
worldNews.content: Governments meeting in Geneva under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons are debating whether to begin negotiations on rules for lethal autonomous weapons. The United States, Russia and Israel oppose a legally binding pact and argue that existing international humanitarian law is sufficient, while the United Kingdom, Germany and France support negotiations on an instrument whose final legal form remains open. The debate concerns systems capable of selecting and attacking targets with reduced direct human control; it is not a general ban on artificial intelligence in defence. UN Secretary-General António Guterres has urged states to establish clear prohibitions and restrictions, citing humanitarian, legal and ethical risks. No treaty has been agreed, and the current talks are about whether to establish a negotiating mandate.

The disagreement is important because European governments argue that any settlement must address their security and Ukraine's future, while Russia wants to shape the negotiating framework. No date has been announced for the next trilateral meeting, and there is no ceasefire agreement. Ukraine also warned of further Russian strikes on infrastructure as winter approaches.

usaNews.summary: Donald Trump is due in Manila for the first Quad leaders' meeting in two years, ahead of an APEC gathering in Shenzhen. Maritime security, critical minerals, export controls and artificial intelligence are among the expected topics.
usaNews.content: US President Donald Trump is travelling to the Philippines as part of an Asia tour that includes a meeting of the Quad — the United States, Japan, Australia and India — and the APEC forum in Shenzhen, China. Reuters reports that the Quad leaders' meeting is the group's first in two years. The agenda is expected to include maritime security, export controls, critical-mineral supply chains and artificial intelligence. The visit comes after Republican losses in US midterm elections and amid renewed scrutiny of a fragile US-China trade truce. Demonstrations in Manila have also criticised the Middle East war and the US-led Pax Silica initiative. Trump is expected to meet Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr and take part in a US-ASEAN special summit, while the Shenzhen programme is expected to bring him into contact with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The trip is a test of whether Washington can reassure regional partners while keeping economic and security channels open with Beijing. Planned meetings should not be treated as completed agreements until official readouts are issued.

usaNews.title: White House warns Democrats over planned probes as new Congress prepares to take control
usaNews.summary: After Democrats won both chambers in the 2026 midterms, White House counsel warned that planned investigations could amount to criminality. Democrats say congressional oversight is a constitutional duty; the new Congress takes office in January 2027.
usaNews.content: The White House has warned Democrats that planned investigations into the Trump administration could amount to what it called “blatant criminality”, escalating a dispute over congressional oversight before the new Congress takes office in January 2027. The Associated Press reports that White House counsel Will Scharf sent a letter to Representative Robert Garcia, the expected incoming House Oversight Committee chair, after Garcia said Trump officials should prepare for scrutiny. Democrats plan investigations into the administration's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files, immigration enforcement, White House construction projects, mineral deals and cryptocurrency activity, among other matters. Garcia rejected the administration's warning and said Congress has constitutional authority to investigate potential wrongdoing. Current Republican committee chair James Comer has also stressed the committee's independence. Democrats won control of both the House and Senate in the midterms, but Republicans remain in control during the lame-duck period until the new Congress is sworn in on 3 January 2027. The White House's warning is a political and legal argument, not a finding that any planned investigation is criminal.

usaNews.title: New US AI-chip export controls unsettle Southeast Asian data-centre investment
usaNews.country: United States / Singapore / Malaysia / Thailand / Indonesia / Brazil
usaNews.summary: New US licensing rules require overseas data centres serving firms in China, Russia, Iran and Cuba to identify end users, and add licensing requirements for chip shipments to several countries including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.
usaNews.content: The Trump administration has introduced new export-control requirements intended to prevent Chinese companies from obtaining restricted American AI computing power through overseas cloud providers. The Associated Press reports that data centres outside the United States serving companies in China, Russia, Iran and Cuba must identify end users, while chip sales to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil face additional licensing requirements because US officials regard those routes as higher risk for diversion. The measures follow scrutiny of possible diversion of Nvidia chips through third-country data centres. Singapore and Malaysia are reviewing possible rerouting of servers and chips and are engaging with US authorities. The controls may raise compliance costs and affect regional data-centre investment, but they are not a general ban on all AI services in Southeast Asia. Firms will need to distinguish lawful cloud access from transactions that require licences or enhanced customer checks.

todaysBigQuestion: What evidence should citizens demand before accepting that a government, political party or international leader has delivered meaningful progress?
thoughtForToday: Trust is earned when public promises can be checked against evidence, accountability and results.
radiantWavesPerspective: Today's stories underline a simple test of public accountability: promises must be measured against evidence and implementation. Lower inflation must translate into improved purchasing power; political reconciliation must respect court orders and party rules; campaign violence allegations require independent investigation; and diplomatic announcements must be tested against written agreements and practical outcomes. RadiantWaves will continue to distinguish verified facts from allegations, official claims, provisional results and proposals still under negotiation.

articles.title: UK maritime monitor reports an unidentified projectile strike near Hormuz as Oman and Iran discuss shipping safety
articles.summary: UKMTO recorded an unidentified projectile striking a merchant vessel near the Strait of Hormuz. Oman and Iran have discussed maritime safety, but no deal restoring normal passage has been announced and the attacker has not been identified.
articles.content: The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency recorded an unidentified projectile striking a merchant vessel near the Strait of Hormuz in Warning 207-26. The warning does not identify the attacker, establish the weapon used or provide grounds for attributing responsibility. Separately, Oman's Foreign Ministry said Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi and Omani officials discussed safeguarding maritime corridors, maintaining the flow of global shipping and reviving dialogue to prevent escalation. Oman has long acted as a mediator and is strategically positioned beside the strait. The talks are important, but they are not a confirmed agreement to reopen normal commercial passage. Ship operators continue to face security warnings, uncertain routes and the possibility of higher freight and insurance costs. Any assessment of the incident must distinguish the UKMTO report of an impact from unverified claims about who was responsible.

articles.background: The Strait of Hormuz links Gulf producers to international markets and is one of the world's most important routes for oil and liquefied natural gas. The current regional conflict has disrupted shipping and increased the risk of miscalculation at sea.
articles.whyItMatters: Even an unattributed strike can raise insurance premiums, delay cargoes and add to energy-price volatility. A durable maritime arrangement would need clear navigation rules, incident reporting and credible security guarantees.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for UKMTO follow-up warnings, independent confirmation of damage, shipping advisories and any written maritime arrangement announced by Oman and Iran.

articles.title: Oil prices ease as recovering Middle East exports offset Gulf security risks
articles.summary: Brent fell 0.8% to US$91.66 a barrel and US WTI slipped 0.9% to US$84.99 in early Tuesday trading. Expectations of a fourth-quarter supply surplus outweighed immediate security concerns, but Hormuz flows remain disrupted.
articles.content: Oil prices fell in early trading on Tuesday as expectations of a fourth-quarter supply surplus outweighed renewed concern about attacks on shipping in the Gulf. Reuters reported Brent crude down 0.8% at US$91.66 a barrel and US West Texas Intermediate down 0.9% at US$84.99. The International Energy Agency expects the market to return to surplus in the fourth quarter as Middle East exports recover faster than demand. That outlook does not mean the security risk has passed. Tanker incidents and the conflict involving Iran continue to threaten shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, where throughput was reported at roughly 49% of pre-war levels. The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve was reported at 276.4 million barrels, its lowest level since August 1982, amid a planned release. For oil-importing economies, including Nigeria, the effect on consumers depends on benchmark prices, exchange rates, domestic pricing and transport costs.

articles.content: European Union foreign ministers meeting in Brussels accused Russia of prolonging negotiations over Ukraine while continuing attacks on power plants and other infrastructure as winter approaches. The Associated Press reports that the EU imposed sanctions on nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions and targeted energy- and oil-linked businesspeople, as well as people accused of spreading pro-Russian disinformation. Ministers said a ceasefire should come before a lasting peace agreement and rejected a Russian-proposed European security framework that they regard as an attempt to weaken NATO. US-led contacts have not produced a lasting ceasefire, and major disagreements remain over territory and future security guarantees. EU leaders have agreed that advisers from France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy and Poland, together with EU officials, should represent Europe in future discussions. The proposed format is not a peace deal. Ukraine's sovereignty and its own decisions remain central to any settlement.

articles.title: France faces another year of weak growth as household purchasing power remains under pressure
articles.summary: Le Monde reports that France's economy has stagnated in 2026, with annual growth expected around 0.4%. Household purchasing power is forecast to fall for a second consecutive year, while the IMF sees only 0.7% growth in 2027.
articles.content: France's economic performance is weakening relative to several European peers. Le Monde reports that gross domestic product contracted slightly in the first and third quarters of 2026, while the European Union as a whole continued to grow. The newspaper cites energy shocks linked to the Middle East conflict, drought and heat, reduced nuclear electricity output, Airbus supply-chain delays, political gridlock and higher borrowing costs among the pressures. Annual growth is expected to reach only about 0.4%, and household purchasing power is forecast to decline for a second year. The International Monetary Fund expects French growth of around 0.7% in 2027. The analysis also points to structural issues, including a comparatively low employment rate among younger and older people. The figures do not mean France is in a recession across every sector, but they underline the challenge facing households, employers and policymakers as public finances limit the room for large-scale support.

articles.content: Prime Minister Andy Burnham used the Lord Mayor's Banquet on 16 November to argue that the UK's hard Brexit settlement had damaged relations with allies and weakened Britain's international standing. In the official speech, he said the government would seek practical agreements at the 20 November UK-EU summit on food and farming, emissions trading and youth mobility, then begin a longer discussion with EU partners about future options. The Guardian reports that those options could include a customs union, the single market or eventual rejoining, while Downing Street says the process will take time and the public will decide. Burnham said any summit deal must remain consistent with the current manifesto and red lines, improve on the existing Brexit settlement and produce measurable benefits in everyday life. The speech is a political direction, not a treaty, a referendum announcement or an immediate change in the UK's legal relationship with the EU. Conservative and pro-Brexit groups are expected to oppose any move that reopens the issue.

Women and children were among those reported dead, and several homes were said to have been destroyed. The Associated Press could not independently verify the death toll. A spokesperson for forces aligned with the army said troops had entered the area and eliminated Rapid Support Forces positions, but did not directly address the reported civilian deaths. Sudan's war between the army and the RSF began in April 2023 and has caused mass displacement, widespread destruction and severe food insecurity. Aid organisations estimate that at least 59,000 people have been killed and around 13 million displaced. The report underscores the risks to civilians as fighting and drone warfare spread across Kordofan and other regions. Responsibility for the specific reported civilian deaths remains disputed and requires independent investigation.

The dispute is unfolding alongside Sudan's devastating war and renewed fighting in Tigray. Analysts warn that cross-border weapons movements and proxy activity could widen the instability. One quarter of contraction does not establish a recession, but it increases scrutiny of real wages, consumption and the timing of further stimulus. Japan's economy is also exposed to disruptions in Gulf energy shipping, making the Strait of Hormuz and regional oil-security plans directly relevant to its outlook. articles.title: COP31 draft decision calls for accelerated action to move away from fossil fuels
articles.summary: Negotiators in Antalya are considering an 18-page draft containing 144 proposals, including language calling for accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels. The text is provisional and remains contested.
articles.content: Climate negotiations at COP31 in Antalya have entered a critical phase, with delegates examining an 18-page draft cover decision containing 144 separate proposals. The draft includes a call for accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels, including an immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems. It also addresses limiting the duration and scale of any overshoot of the 1.5°C temperature threshold and accelerating clean electrification. The wording is not final: negotiators remain divided over climate finance, adaptation, the proposed just-transition mechanism and how commitments should be implemented. Campaigners warn that ambitious language could be weakened before adoption, while developing countries continue to demand accessible funding to manage climate impacts. The United Nations says COP31 runs from 9 to 20 November in Antalya, and the resumed high-level segment takes place on 17 and 18 November. The key test is whether governments can turn draft language into funded, measurable action.

articles.title: Nigeria's October inflation eases to 14.06%, but food inflation and household costs remain high

articles.content: Nigeria's annual headline inflation rate eased to 14.06% in October from 14.63% in September, according to National Bureau of Statistics data reported by Reuters. Food inflation slowed to 19.13% from 19.59%. The figures suggest that the pace of price increases is moderating, but they do not mean food, transport, rent or energy have become cheaper. Households are still paying prices shaped by earlier inflation and by the effects of fuel and foreign-exchange reforms. The government will need to demonstrate that the improvement is sustained and reaches ordinary consumers through lower food supply costs, better transport access, more jobs and stronger real wages. Opposition parties are entitled to scrutinise the figures, but claims of either complete economic recovery or total statistical failure should be tested against the published methodology and household experience.

Four assemblies were expected to submit their reports by 17 November. The 32 reported approvals exceed the two-thirds threshold required for a constitutional alteration, but the public record should not be described as a verified 36-of-36 approval until the outstanding reports are formally confirmed. The bill could move towards transmission to the President, but it is not yet an operational state-police service. Important questions remain about appointments, funding, jurisdiction, federal-state coordination, independent complaints bodies and safeguards against political abuse. Decentralised policing may improve local intelligence, but weak oversight could expose officers to pressure from governors or local power brokers.

The minister warned that Islamic State Sahel was seeking to recruit criminal gangs in northwestern Nigeria. These statements come amid a long-running insurgency in the northeast, rising attacks by Boko Haram and ISWAP, banditry and kidnappings. The defence minister's account is an official statement; independent operational assessments and casualty verification remain important. Security cooperation may improve surveillance and coordination, but lasting safety also depends on civilian protection, accountable operations, local trust and addressing the conditions that allow armed groups to recruit.

articles.title: France's public-sector unions stage nationwide strike over pay and purchasing power
articles.summary: Eight public-sector unions have called a national strike and demonstrations on 17 November over pay and purchasing power. The government has offered targeted measures for lower-paid staff but has not agreed to a general increase in the civil-service index point.
articles.content: Eight public-sector unions in France — CGT, FO, CFDT, UNSA, FSU, Solidaires, CFE-CGC and FA-FP — have called workers to strike and demonstrate on Tuesday, 17 November. Their central demand is an immediate improvement in pay and a rise in the civil-service index point, which has been frozen since July 2023. Le Monde reports that the unions regard the government's targeted measures for lower-paid employees as insufficient, particularly because the minimum-wage increase due on 1 December will leave the base pay of many public employees below the new SMIC. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has opened a one-month discussion on five areas, including emergency measures for low salaries, and has scheduled another meeting with unions for 11 December. The government argues that a general increase would be costly and is prioritising targeted support. articles.title: Marine Le Pen due to present pension proposals as investors question National Rally's savings arithmetic
articles.summary: Marine Le Pen is due to present pension proposals on Tuesday. The National Rally says its plan could save €15–20 billion a year while allowing some early starters to retire at 60–62, but investors question whether the savings are compatible with reversing the 2023 reform.
articles.content: Marine Le Pen is due to present pension proposals as the National Rally seeks to reassure investors before France's 2027 presidential election. The party has promised to let some workers who began employment young retire between 60 and 62 after 40 to 42 years of contributions, while also pledging €15 billion to €20 billion in annual pension savings and €140 billion in wider budget savings by 2032. Reuters reports that economists and investors question whether those targets can be achieved if the party reverses Emmanuel Macron's 2023 reform, which raised the statutory retirement age from 62 to 64. The RN's recent emphasis on contribution years could mean many university graduates work into their 60s to receive full benefits. Pensions are France's largest public spending item, forecast at more than €430 billion next year. The detailed proposal had not yet been published at the time of this morning briefing; the figures are campaign claims, not independently verified savings or government policy.

articles.title: Le Pen's proposal to end French financial aid to Ukraine exposes a major 2027 foreign-policy divide
articles.summary: Le Pen says an RN government would end French financial aid to Ukraine within six months of taking office. Macron warns that cutting support could pressure Kyiv into an unjust peace; the proposal is not current policy.
articles.content: Marine Le Pen has defended a proposal to end French financial support for Ukraine within six months if the National Rally wins the 2027 presidential election. She argues that France's public finances cannot sustain the current level of assistance, while allowing that some material support or military training could continue. Le Monde reports that France's bilateral and European contributions since 2022 amount to about €27 billion. President Emmanuel Macron says withdrawing support could leave Ukraine under pressure to accept an unjust settlement. The proposal would affect France's role in European aid mechanisms and its influence over future negotiations. It is an election position, not a decision by the current French government. Its implementation would depend on the election result, parliamentary arrangements and France's European commitments.

articles.title: Turkey appoints trustee to pro-opposition Sözcü TV as executives are detained
articles.summary: Reuters reports that police raided pro-opposition Sözcü TV and its website, detained executives and appointed the state deposit-insurance fund as trustee. The outlet says its print newspaper is outside the order; the legal allegations remain under investigation.
articles.content: Turkish police raided the Istanbul headquarters of pro-opposition Sözcü TV and its website early on Tuesday, and a trustee was appointed to oversee the broadcaster and the online outlet, according to Sözcü and Reuters. The outlet reported that its chairwoman and other executives were detained, while its print newspaper and two associated publications were not covered by the trusteeship order. A separate report summarising a statement from the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office says investigators examined financial-crime reports and alleged that companies linked to the media group were financed through overseas bank accounts associated with a person accused of FETÖ/PDY links; detention orders were issued for four people. Those are allegations in an investigation, not findings of guilt. Reuters said the government did not immediately comment on the latest operation. The precise scope of the trusteeship and the legal grounds should be assessed against the court order and prosecutor's statement, not political claims alone.

articles.content: China's Foreign Ministry has confirmed that President Xi Jinping will hold a China-Russia-United States summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen on 19 November. The announcement makes the meeting a major diplomatic event during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation gathering. The three governments have not published a joint agenda or agreed outcome. Washington has signalled interest in nuclear arms control and wider strategic issues, while Beijing describes the meeting in terms of strategic stability and cooperation. The Ukraine war, sanctions, Taiwan, trade and energy security are likely to shape the political context, but should not be presented as confirmed agenda items until the participants say so. articles.title: Oman and Iran discuss safeguarding maritime corridors, but no Hormuz reopening deal is announced
articles.summary: Oman's Foreign Ministry says the two countries discussed shipping safety and dialogue during Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi's visit. The talks produced no confirmed agreement to reopen normal traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
articles.content: Oman and Iran have discussed safeguarding maritime corridors and maintaining the flow of global shipping and trade, according to Oman's Foreign Ministry. The talks took place during Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi's visit to Muscat. Oman has long acted as a mediator and controls the southern shore of the Strait of Hormuz, while Iran has sought greater control over routes through the waterway. The discussions come amid tanker attacks, a US naval blockade and wider negotiations over the conflict. No final agreement to restore unrestricted commercial passage was announced. The strait carried about one-fifth of global energy supplies before the conflict, so any durable arrangement would require clarity on navigation, mine risks, insurance, military activity and the rights of commercial vessels.

articles.title: Canada and China extend trade concessions as Carney seeks alternatives to US market dependence
articles.summary: Canada and China have expanded a preliminary trade arrangement. Beijing will reduce tariffs on about C$400 million of Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports, while Ottawa extends tariff-remission measures for some Chinese steel and aluminium products for two years.
articles.content: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to extend and expand a preliminary trade arrangement during a meeting in Shenzhen ahead of the APEC summit. Reuters reports that China will reduce tariffs on about C$400 million of Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports. Canada will extend for two years remission measures for some Chinese steel and aluminium products. Carney said Canada was ahead of schedule on its goal of increasing exports to China by 50% by 2030, as his government seeks to diversify markets and reduce dependence on the United States. The arrangement is not a comprehensive free-trade agreement. It also does not erase concerns raised by security analysts and human-rights groups about alleged Chinese election interference, coercive trade practices and the treatment of dissidents. Beijing rejects accusations of interference in Canada's domestic affairs. The trade concessions create opportunities for exporters, but implementation and domestic political scrutiny will matter.

articles.title: White House warns Democrats over planned probes as new Congress prepares to take control
articles.summary: After Democrats won both chambers in the 2026 midterms, White House counsel warned that planned investigations could amount to criminality. Democrats say congressional oversight is a constitutional duty; the new Congress takes office in January 2027.
articles.content: The White House has warned Democrats that planned investigations into the Trump administration could amount to what it called “blatant criminality”, escalating a dispute over congressional oversight before the new Congress takes office in January 2027. The Associated Press reports that White House counsel Will Scharf sent a letter to Representative Robert Garcia, the expected incoming House Oversight Committee chair, after Garcia said Trump officials should prepare for scrutiny. Democrats plan investigations into the administration's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files, immigration enforcement, White House construction projects, mineral deals and cryptocurrency activity, among other matters. Garcia rejected the administration's warning and said Congress has constitutional authority to investigate potential wrongdoing. Current Republican committee chair James Comer has also stressed the committee's independence. Democrats won control of both the House and Senate in the midterms, but Republicans remain in control during the lame-duck period until the new Congress is sworn in on 3 January 2027. The White House's warning is a political and legal argument, not a finding that any planned investigation is criminal.

articles.title: New US AI-chip export controls unsettle Southeast Asian data-centre investment

articles.content: The Trump administration has introduced new export-control requirements intended to prevent Chinese companies from obtaining restricted American AI computing power through overseas cloud providers. The Associated Press reports that data centres outside the United States serving companies in China, Russia, Iran and Cuba must identify end users, while chip sales to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil face additional licensing requirements because US officials regard those routes as higher risk for diversion. The measures follow scrutiny of possible diversion of Nvidia chips through third-country data centres. Singapore and Malaysia are reviewing possible rerouting of servers and chips and are engaging with US authorities. The controls may raise compliance costs and affect regional data-centre investment, but they are not a general ban on all AI services in Southeast Asia. Firms will need to distinguish lawful cloud access from transactions that require licences or enhanced customer checks.

articles.title: EBRD warns developing economies risk missing the productivity gains of the AI boom
articles.summary: The EBRD's Transition Report 2026–27 warns that many developing economies may miss opportunities from artificial intelligence and higher defence spending because of weak electricity networks, limited finance and industrial capacity.
articles.content: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development's Transition Report 2026–27, published on 17 November, warns that developing economies could miss the economic opportunities created by artificial intelligence and rising defence spending. Chief economist Beata Javorcik says many countries lack reliable electricity, finance, industrial capacity and the research base needed to compete in complex sectors such as advanced AI hardware and defence systems. In nearly half of the EBRD countries covered, electricity grids may not support even one data centre, according to the report's findings as reported by Reuters. The report does not suggest that emerging economies have no options: lower-barrier AI applications, drones, software services and specialised manufacturing may offer entry points if governments invest in skills, infrastructure and institutions. For African economies, access to reliable power, digital skills, local-language tools and data protection will shape whether AI supports productivity or deepens dependence on imported technology.

articles.summary: The ECDC's 16 November update recorded 11,376 confirmed cases and 5,568 related deaths in the DRC, using data through 14 November. Nigeria's single reported case was discharged on 11 November and all 62 identified contacts completed monitoring.
articles.content: The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control's 16 November update recorded 11,376 confirmed cases and 5,568 related deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, using data available through 14 November. Community transmission continues across eight provinces. The update also says one Ebola case was reported in Nigeria on 20 October in a person with travel history to Uganda; the patient was medically evacuated to Switzerland and discharged on 11 November. All 62 identified contacts in Nigeria completed monitoring on 11 November, while one contact remained in quarantine in Switzerland. Kenya had reported nine confirmed cases, including two deaths, all linked to its first case; the last case was reported on 20 October. These figures are tied to the ECDC's reporting cut-off and should not be presented as real-time totals. Nigeria's completed contact monitoring is reassuring, but it does not remove the need for surveillance, infection prevention and cross-border coordination.

The constitutional framework currently in force does not impose a presidential term limit because a proposed new constitution containing limits failed to pass in 2020. Barrow says the opposition prevented the reform; critics argue that the failed process left an important democratic safeguard unresolved. The election will test whether the electoral commission can ensure equal campaign access, transparent counting and credible dispute resolution. Barrow's eligibility under the current rules is distinct from the political argument over whether a two-term limit should be introduced.

articles.title: Japan protests after two suspected Russian aircraft briefly violate its airspace
articles.summary: Japan's Defence Ministry says two suspected Russian aircraft entered its airspace near Okinoshima for about three minutes each. Japanese fighters scrambled and Tokyo lodged a formal protest.
articles.content: Japan's Defence Ministry says two aircraft believed to be Russian entered Japanese airspace northwest of Okinoshima, off Fukuoka, early Tuesday. The first incursion was recorded from about 4:07 to 4:10 a.m.; the second from about 4:09 to 4:12 a.m. Japan's Air Self-Defense Force scrambled fighters and issued warnings. Tokyo said it lodged a strong protest with Moscow and demanded measures to prevent a recurrence. The aircraft later crossed the Tsushima Strait and passed between Yonaguni and Taiwan into the Pacific. The ministry did not identify the aircraft types. The incident comes amid heightened Russian-Chinese military activity near Japan and ahead of the planned Xi-Trump-Putin summit in Shenzhen. Russia's response to the protest had not been reported at the time of this edition.

articles.title: UN Geneva talks remain divided over legally binding limits on autonomous weapons

articles.summary: States meeting in Geneva remain divided over whether to negotiate a binding protocol on lethal autonomous weapons. The US, Russia and Israel oppose a binding pact; several European states support negotiations.
articles.content: Governments meeting in Geneva under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons are debating whether to begin negotiations on rules for lethal autonomous weapons. The United States, Russia and Israel oppose a legally binding pact and argue that existing international humanitarian law is sufficient, while the United Kingdom, Germany and France support negotiations on an instrument whose final legal form remains open. The debate concerns systems capable of selecting and attacking targets with reduced direct human control; it is not a general ban on artificial intelligence in defence. UN Secretary-General António Guterres has urged states to establish clear prohibitions and restrictions, citing humanitarian, legal and ethical risks. No treaty has been agreed, and the current talks are about whether to establish a negotiating mandate.

articles.content: Renault has announced a restructuring in France that includes 1,090 voluntary departures in 2027 and about 2,000 hires, mainly in digital, robotics and electronics. The company says it must improve productivity and shorten vehicle-development times as Chinese competitors become more aggressive on price and development speed. About half of the departures are expected in engineering, while planned hiring and expansion will be distributed unevenly across sites. The company says factories in Douai, Maubeuge and Sandouville will gain positions, while other sites face job reductions or no replacement hiring. Unions question whether all planned recruitment will materialise amid economic uncertainty. The announcement is a corporate plan, not a guarantee that every advertised job is already open.

articles.content: Japan has proposed an Asia-wide oil-security task force to coordinate strategic stockpiles and emergency supply releases after the conflict around the Strait of Hormuz exposed the region's dependence on Gulf energy. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told Southeast Asian leaders in Manila that Japan could make use of idle storage capacity and work with a Philippine-led joint stockpiling scheme. She described the idea as a possible Asian counterpart to the International Energy Agency and also proposed a Power Gulf Initiative to strengthen ties between Middle Eastern producers and Asian consumers. Reuters reports that around 90% of crude oil shipped through the Strait of Hormuz is destined for Asia. The proposal is not yet an operating regional reserve or a binding commitment to release oil. It would require agreed membership, financing, access rules, information-sharing and emergency procedures.

europeNews.title: EU accuses Russia of prolonging Ukraine war and imposes new sanctions
europeNews.summary: EU foreign ministers accused Moscow of dragging out peace talks while attacking Ukrainian infrastructure and agreed sanctions targeting nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions, alongside individuals and energy-linked business interests.
europeNews.content: European Union foreign ministers meeting in Brussels accused Russia of prolonging negotiations over Ukraine while continuing attacks on power plants and other infrastructure as winter approaches. The Associated Press reports that the EU imposed sanctions on nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions and targeted energy- and oil-linked businesspeople, as well as people accused of spreading pro-Russian disinformation. Ministers said a ceasefire should come before a lasting peace agreement and rejected a Russian-proposed European security framework that they regard as an attempt to weaken NATO. US-led contacts have not produced a lasting ceasefire, and major disagreements remain over territory and future security guarantees. EU leaders have agreed that advisers from France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy and Poland, together with EU officials, should represent Europe in future discussions. The proposed format is not a peace deal. Ukraine's sovereignty and its own decisions remain central to any settlement.

europeNews.title: France faces another year of weak growth as household purchasing power remains under pressure
europeNews.summary: Le Monde reports that France's economy has stagnated in 2026, with annual growth expected around 0.4%. Household purchasing power is forecast to fall for a second consecutive year, while the IMF sees only 0.7% growth in 2027.
europeNews.content: France's economic performance is weakening relative to several European peers. Le Monde reports that gross domestic product contracted slightly in the first and third quarters of 2026, while the European Union as a whole continued to grow. The newspaper cites energy shocks linked to the Middle East conflict, drought and heat, reduced nuclear electricity output, Airbus supply-chain delays, political gridlock and higher borrowing costs among the pressures. Annual growth is expected to reach only about 0.4%, and household purchasing power is forecast to decline for a second year. The International Monetary Fund expects French growth of around 0.7% in 2027. The analysis also points to structural issues, including a comparatively low employment rate among younger and older people. The figures do not mean France is in a recession across every sector, but they underline the challenge facing households, employers and policymakers as public finances limit the room for large-scale support.

europeNews.title: Burnham says Brexit weakened Britain's global standing and opens debate on the UK's long-term EU relationship
europeNews.summary: In a 16 November speech, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain's global standing had diminished since Brexit. He plans to begin a discussion on long-term options after the 20 November UK-EU summit; no immediate return to the EU has been announced.
europeNews.content: Prime Minister Andy Burnham used the Lord Mayor's Banquet on 16 November to argue that the UK's hard Brexit settlement had damaged relations with allies and weakened Britain's international standing. In the official speech, he said the government would seek practical agreements at the 20 November UK-EU summit on food and farming, emissions trading and youth mobility, then begin a longer discussion with EU partners about future options. The Guardian reports that those options could include a customs union, the single market or eventual rejoining, while Downing Street says the process will take time and the public will decide. Burnham said any summit deal must remain consistent with the current manifesto and red lines, improve on the existing Brexit settlement and produce measurable benefits in everyday life. The speech is a political direction, not a treaty, a referendum announcement or an immediate change in the UK's legal relationship with the EU. Conservative and pro-Brexit groups are expected to oppose any move that reopens the issue.

europeNews.summary: Berlin has called for faster and more reliable humanitarian access to Gaza. Aid agencies continue to warn that shelter, medical supplies and basic services remain inadequate.

Israeli authorities say security screening is necessary to prevent weapons and materials reaching armed groups; humanitarian agencies argue that delays and restrictions are preventing aid from reaching civilians at the scale required. The latest diplomatic call does not itself change border procedures or guarantee additional deliveries. Aid organisations continue to stress that civilians must be protected and that humanitarian access should be safe, sustained and independent of political bargaining.

europeNews.title: France's public-sector unions stage nationwide strike over pay and purchasing power
europeNews.summary: Eight public-sector unions have called a national strike and demonstrations on 17 November over pay and purchasing power. The government has offered targeted measures for lower-paid staff but has not agreed to a general increase in the civil-service index point.
europeNews.content: Eight public-sector unions in France — CGT, FO, CFDT, UNSA, FSU, Solidaires, CFE-CGC and FA-FP — have called workers to strike and demonstrate on Tuesday, 17 November. Their central demand is an immediate improvement in pay and a rise in the civil-service index point, which has been frozen since July 2023. Le Monde reports that the unions regard the government's targeted measures for lower-paid employees as insufficient, particularly because the minimum-wage increase due on 1 December will leave the base pay of many public employees below the new SMIC. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has opened a one-month discussion on five areas, including emergency measures for low salaries, and has scheduled another meeting with unions for 11 December. The government argues that a general increase would be costly and is prioritising targeted support. The scale of participation and disruption to schools, transport and public services is still being assessed; local effects will vary. The mobilisation is a labour dispute and should not be presented as a general call for the government's resignation.

europeNews.title: Marine Le Pen due to present pension proposals as investors question National Rally's savings arithmetic
europeNews.summary: Marine Le Pen is due to present pension proposals on Tuesday. The National Rally says its plan could save €15–20 billion a year while allowing some early starters to retire at 60–62, but investors question whether the savings are compatible with reversing the 2023 reform.
europeNews.content: Marine Le Pen is due to present pension proposals as the National Rally seeks to reassure investors before France's 2027 presidential election. The party has promised to let some workers who began employment young retire between 60 and 62 after 40 to 42 years of contributions, while also pledging €15 billion to €20 billion in annual pension savings and €140 billion in wider budget savings by 2032. Reuters reports that economists and investors question whether those targets can be achieved if the party reverses Emmanuel Macron's 2023 reform, which raised the statutory retirement age from 62 to 64. The RN's recent emphasis on contribution years could mean many university graduates work into their 60s to receive full benefits. Pensions are France's largest public spending item, forecast at more than €430 billion next year. The detailed proposal had not yet been published at the time of this morning briefing; the figures are campaign claims, not independently verified savings or government policy.

Le Monde reports that France's bilateral and European contributions since 2022 amount to about €27 billion. President Emmanuel Macron says withdrawing support could leave Ukraine under pressure to accept an unjust settlement. The proposal would affect France's role in European aid mechanisms and its influence over future negotiations. It is an election position, not a decision by the current French government. Its implementation would depend on the election result, parliamentary arrangements and France's European commitments.

europeNews.title: Turkey appoints trustee to pro-opposition Sözcü TV as executives are detained

europeNews.summary: Renault says it plans 1,090 voluntary departures in 2027 and 2,000 hires, mainly in digital, robotics and electronics, as it restructures to compete with Chinese manufacturers.

About half of the departures are expected in engineering, while planned hiring and expansion will be distributed unevenly across sites. The company says factories in Douai, Maubeuge and Sandouville will gain positions, while other sites face job reductions or no replacement hiring. africaNews.title: Sudan rights group reports at least 13 killed in West Kordofan airstrike
africaNews.summary: Emergency Lawyers says a Sudanese army airstrike killed at least 13 people, including women and children, in West Kordofan. The Associated Press says it could not independently verify the reported death toll.
africaNews.content: A local rights group, Emergency Lawyers, says at least 13 people were killed when a Sudanese army airstrike hit the Abu Qalb area of West Kordofan. Women and children were among those reported dead, and several homes were said to have been destroyed. The Associated Press could not independently verify the death toll. A spokesperson for forces aligned with the army said troops had entered the area and eliminated Rapid Support Forces positions, but did not directly address the reported civilian deaths. Sudan's war between the army and the RSF began in April 2023 and has caused mass displacement, widespread destruction and severe food insecurity. Aid organisations estimate that at least 59,000 people have been killed and around 13 million displaced. The report underscores the risks to civilians as fighting and drone warfare spread across Kordofan and other regions. Responsibility for the specific reported civilian deaths remains disputed and requires independent investigation.

Sudan has raised its claims with the United Nations and African Union, while Ethiopia has expelled six Sudanese consular staff and closed the mission. The dispute is unfolding alongside Sudan's devastating war and renewed fighting in Tigray. Analysts warn that cross-border weapons movements and proxy activity could widen the instability. The allegations must remain attributed claims rather than established facts. Regional diplomacy is urgently needed to prevent the two conflicts from becoming more closely connected.
